title: 1 Samuel 31:1–7
context: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa, killing Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua; Saul, badly wounded by archers, asks his armor bearer to kill him, and when the armor bearer refuses in fear, Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor bearer does the same. Saul dies with his three sons, his armor bearer, and his men that day, and the Israelites across the valley abandon their cities. Both traditions read this as a sober and grievous end to Saul’s reign, fulfilling the word of 28:19, and they handle the manner of his death pastorally; the different account given later by an Amalekite in 2 Samuel 1 is noted without harmonizing beyond the text.

verses.text: Now the Philistines fought against Israel; and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain on Mount Gilboa.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines fight Israel, and the men of Israel flee and fall slain on Mount Gilboa. Arminian readers note that the narrative shifts from David’s victory to Saul’s defeat, placing the two side by side.

The parallel account appears in 1 Chronicles 10:1–14.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the fulfillment of Samuel’s word to Saul the night before (1 Sam 28:19).

The contrast between the two chapters is deliberate: David seeks the LORD and recovers all, while Saul, who received no answer (28:6), loses all.

verses.text: The Philistines overtook Saul and his sons; and the Philistines killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines kill Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul’s sons. Arminian readers note the grief of Jonathan’s death in particular, given his friendship with David and his faithfulness.

David will lament Jonathan and Saul together (2 Sam 1:17–27).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the tragedy of Jonathan dying alongside his father.

The faithful son shares in the judgment on his father’s house, which reminds readers that the consequences of a leader’s sin often fall on others.

verses.text: The battle went hard against Saul, and the archers overtook him; and he was greatly distressed by reason of the archers.
verses.arminianNotes:
The battle goes hard against Saul, and the archers wound him badly. Arminian readers note the vulnerability of the once-imposing king.

The narrator describes his distress without excess detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the end of Saul’s reign approaching as God’s word comes to pass.

Saul is “greatly distressed,” the same kind of language used of David in 30:6; the difference lies in where each turns.

verses.text: Then Saul said to his armor bearer, “Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through and abuse me!” But his armor bearer would not, for he was terrified. Therefore Saul took his sword and fell on it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul asks his armor bearer to kill him so that the uncircumcised will not abuse him; when the armor bearer refuses out of fear, Saul falls on his own sword. Arminian readers handle the scene pastorally, noting Saul’s fear of humiliation (cf. Judg 16:23–25).

The text describes what happened without commenting on Saul’s eternal state, and readers should do the same.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the account soberly and do not speculate about Saul’s final destiny.

The armor bearer’s refusal may reflect reverence for the LORD’s anointed, as David also refused to harm Saul (1 Sam 24:6; 26:9), though the text says only that he was terrified. 2 Samuel 1:6–10 gives an Amalekite’s different account; this note does not harmonize the two.

verses.text: When his armor bearer saw that Saul was dead, he likewise fell on his sword, and died with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The armor bearer, seeing that Saul is dead, falls on his sword and dies with him. Arminian readers note the loyalty and despair shown in his act.

The text records his death briefly and with restraint.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read the scene with sorrow and restraint.

Scripture records a few such deaths (cf. Judg 9:54; 2 Sam 17:23) without offering a full theology of them, so pastoral care and caution are fitting.

verses.text: So Saul died with his three sons, his armor bearer, and all his men that same day together.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul dies with his three sons, his armor bearer, and all his men that same day. Arminian readers note the completeness of the disaster for Saul’s house and army.

The narrator’s summary is grave and simple.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the word of 28:19 fulfilled. 1 Chronicles 10:13–14 gives a theological summary of Saul’s death in terms of unfaithfulness to the LORD.

Both traditions treat the verse with sobriety and avoid judgment beyond what Scripture says.

verses.text: When the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley, and those who were beyond the Jordan, saw that the men of Israel fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned the cities and fled; and the Philistines came and lived in them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israelites across the valley and beyond the Jordan see the defeat, abandon their cities, and the Philistines occupy them. Arminian readers note the wide consequences of the king’s fall.

The people suffer when leadership collapses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the land left exposed and the need for a new king God has already chosen.

The chapter’s grim picture prepares for David’s reign, through which God will restore Israel.
